extracted.intended_audience: improv performers, troupe organizers, and improv show producers
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and production/guidance for running and performing Theatresports — a judged team improv competition format (includes core rules, judging procedures, scoring, timing, penalties, and common variations).

rubrics_metrics.name: MC introduction and warm-up
rubrics_metrics.description: The game is introduced by an MC, who does a warm-up and then introduces the judges and the 2 teams
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MC should open the show with a warm-up and formally introduce judges and the competing teams to set the stage for the format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judges lead the game
rubrics_metrics.description: The game is lead by judges
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges control flow, enforce rules, issue warnings/penalties, and interpret audience response; they are central to managing each challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed duration per game
rubrics_metrics.description: Each game has a fixed duration
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every challenge/scenario is allotted a set time so the show stays on schedule; timing is enforced by the judges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deciding which team starts
rubrics_metrics.description: A toss decides which team starts with a challenge
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a fair random method (coin toss) to determine which team issues the first challenge; establishes impartiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Challengers go first and define challenge scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Challengers go first. Possible challenges are the classic games, but anything goes. One might challenge the other team to play the dullest scene possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenging team sets the challenge; challenges can be imaginative or subversive (e.g., 'play the dullest scene') — creativity in challenges is allowed within house norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to protest (baulk) a challenge
rubrics_metrics.description: Teams can protest or baulk at a challenge. The judges may accept the baulk, in which case the challengers need to come up with a new challenge. Reason for baulking at a challenge might be 'we`ve already done this game tonight'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teams may object to a challenge; judges adjudicate whether the objection is valid and can require a new challenge if accepted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Horn warning for boring
rubrics_metrics.description: The judges carry a horn, which they use to issue a warning for boring. After a warning the scene should be concluded ASAP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a scene is flagged as boring by judges, they sound the horn and the performers must wrap up quickly to keep show quality and pace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalties for misconduct or poor form
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges can issue penalties, for e.g. obscenities, smart-assing or whatever.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges may penalize behavior that violates house rules, standards, or decorum; examples include obscenities or excessive smart-assing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punishment mechanic (basket over head)
rubrics_metrics.description: A punished player gets a basket over his head for a number of minutes
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Troupes may use playful physical penalties (e.g., basket over head) to enforce judgments; length of punishment is at judges' discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scenes must end on time with judge time-calls
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenes must end on time; the judges indicate the time, and warn the players e.g. when they got 30 seconds left. Or they honk a warning for boring, after which the scene must end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges manage timing, give explicit countdown warnings (e.g., 30 seconds left), and use the horn or other signals to ensure scenes finish promptly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience-based winner determination (interpreted by judges)
rubrics_metrics.description: After each challenge (played by both teams) the audience decided by means of cheering, yelling of applause which team won, as interpreted by the judges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audience reaction (cheers/applause) is the primary input for deciding winners, but judges have final interpretation to resolve disputes or close calls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point scoring for wins
rubrics_metrics.description: Winners get 5 points, losers get nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A simple scoring scheme assigns 5 points to the winning team for each judged challenge; losing team receives 0 points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical show length
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole show lasts about 45 minutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan the evening's pacing and number of challenges around an approximately 45-minute total runtime for the main show.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation: judges issue challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: Some troupes let the judges issue the challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of team-issued challenges, judges may propose challenges to ensure variety, fairness, or to control difficulty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation: winning team free scene
rubrics_metrics.description: Other troupes allow the winning team a free scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As an incentive, some formats permit the winning team to perform an additional unjudged/free scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danish variety: single Ombuds role
rubrics_metrics.description: Danish variety: in this format there is only one judge, called an Ombuds. The Ombuds is both Commentator, MC and scorekeeper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Danish variant simplifies roles into one person who handles commentary, MC duties, and scoring — suitable for smaller troupes or beginners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of props, décor, and effects
rubrics_metrics.description: This format is quite often played with props, in a décor. Sound and light effects are also used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate props, set dressing, sound, and lighting to enhance scenes and theatricality when appropriate for the troupe and venue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danish version suitability for beginners
rubrics_metrics.description: The Danish version is a bit simpler, and can be used to play with beginners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the simpler Danish rules and single-judge format as an entry-level version to introduce new players to Theatresports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Programming an evening (Danish warm-up then full show)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some troupes start an evening off with a 20-minute Danish game, and then play a 45-minute full version after the intermission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure a show by using a shorter Danish-format opener as a warm-up for players and audience, followed by a longer full Theatresports set post-intermission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark and origin attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Theatresports is a registered trademark by Keith Johnstone. A complete overview can be found in his book Impro for Storytellers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge the trademark and consult Keith Johnstone's 'Impro for Storytellers' for authoritative rules and history; respect trademark attribution where applicable.
